newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FORECAST - NZ election and likely policy changes.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - NZ election and likely policy changes.

text.p: A Reuters poll of 10 New Zealand bankers, fund managers, stockbrokers and economists shows most see slower debt repayment and a widening of the Reserve Bank's 0-2 percent target band for inflation as the most likely policy changes after Saturday's election.
The 10 were split on the likely election outcome.

Five expected the conservative National Party to remain in power, but differed on whether it would form a one-party minority government, a minority coalition with one or more smaller parties or a majority centre-right coalition.
Four respondents expected a Labour-led coalition. Two predicted a two-party government with economic nationalist New Zealand First, while two saw a three-way coalition with the left-wing Alliance.
One said the election was simply too close to call, and if National failed to form a majority coalition it could take some months for an alternative to emerge.
Most were unwilling to be named, and most replies were received before two weekend opinion polls showing Labour's support firming at the expense of National.
Asked to say what possible policy and legislative changes worried them most, respondents gave the following overall ranking (with one indicating greatest concern and 10 least).
GREATEST CONCERNS

1. Introduction of Alliance-style financial transactions tax at rate of 10 cents in every hundred dollars, replacing Goods and Services Tax 2. Amend Reserve Bank Act to target employment and sustainable economic growth as well as price stability. 3. Significant rise in government spending. 4. Curbs on foreign investment. 5. Raising of import tariffs (as proposed by

Alliance). 6. Repeal of Employment Contracts Act deregulating the labour market (as favoured by Labour and Alliance). 7. Slower rate of repayment of public debt. 8. Restrictions on land purchase by foreigners. 9. Widening of Reserve Bank target range for underlying inflation but retaining focus on price stability (as proposed by Labour). 10. Introduction of compulsory superannuation (as proposed by New Zealand First).

The top six concerns were ranked quite evenly, but respondents were noticeably more relaxed about the rest. Only one ranked a widening of the Reserve Bank target band (currently 0-2 percent) in his top five.
Respondents were asked separately to say which of the 10 policy changes was the most likely to occur in practice.
MOST LIKELY CHANGES
The closest correlation between the two sets of answers was for significant rise in government spending (third greatest concern and third most likely outcome).
TOP PRIORITIES FOR AN INCOMING GOVERNMENT
Verbatim extracts from replies:
-- Overvalued currency starting to damage exporters (especially primary producers)
-- Inflation target band that is too narrow

1. Slower public debt repayment (eight respondents out of 10). 2. Widen RBNZ target band but keep price stability focus (six). 3. Significant rise in government spending (five). 4. Compulsory superannuation (three). 5= Repeal of Employment Contracts Act (one) 5= Make RBNZ target employment, sustainable growth (one) Note - Some respondents listed more than one likely change.
In general, respondents seemed to believe the changes that concerned them most were the least likely to occur in practice.
-- Why does New Zealand need short-term rates at 10 percent to keep inflation sub-three percent when most of the OECD manage with rates between three and six percent?
-- Health and education reform; lack of willingness of even National Party to open the door wider to private provision and consumer choice.
-- Maintain current policy, keep inflation under control, continue with tax cuts, bring in compulsory superannuation.
-- Establishing an appropriate monetary and fiscal policy mix to ensure the sustainability of the economic expansion.
-- Maintain confidence that the overall framework of economic policy will remain intact even though particular areas may well change, e.g. labour market, Employment Contracts Act

-- Stability. A small economy highly dependent upon overseas trade and global investment for its ability to grow and create wealth needs, above all else, stability in both monetary and fiscal management.

-- Preserve the current direction of economic policy -- namely progressive debt reduction and surpluses remaining at three percent or so of GDP per annum. Some easing in the (inflation target) is inevitable but not a big negative.
Pressure will be on to increase government expenditure.

-- Maintain overall sense of stability and certainty in leadership. Continuance of current economic direction including changes to maintain the competitiveness of the NZ economy to keep pace with global changes. Above this the financial markets would look favourably upon further reforms to tariffs and repayment of public debt.
